items.question: What is the temporal dead zone (TDZ)?
items.answer: The period from entering a block until a let or const declaration runs where the binding exists in the lexical environment but cannot be accessed. Reading it throws ReferenceError. var has no TDZ — it hoists to undefined instead. C# catches use-before-declare at compile time; JavaScript throws at run time for let/const.
followUps: Why does for (let i...) fix closure-in-loop bugs?
Does const make objects deeply immutable?
items.sixtySeconds: TDZ = let/const hoisted uninitialized until their line. Access before = ReferenceError. var hoists to undefined. Default const, let to reassign, avoid var.

items.question: Does JavaScript if() treat 0 as false like truthiness?
items.answer: Yes. if accepts any value and applies ToBoolean. Zero, empty string, null, undefined, NaN, false, -0, and 0n are falsy. Everything else — including [] and {} — is truthy. C# requires bool in if conditions; this is the biggest mindset shift for C# developers.
followUps: How does switch compare case values?
items.sixtySeconds: Eight falsy values. Empty array truthy. Prefer explicit compares (count > 0). switch uses === strict equality.

items.question: What is the difference between ?? and ||?
items.answer: ?? returns the right side only when the left is null or undefined. || returns the right side when the left is any falsy value including 0, "", and false. Use ?? for API defaults where 0 or empty string are valid. Use || only when all falsy values should fall through.
followUps: What is the precedence of ?? versus ||?
items.sixtySeconds: ?? = nullish only. || = all falsy. 0 ?? 10 stays 0; 0 || 10 becomes 10. Parenthesize ?? with ||.

items.question: When do you use for...of versus for...in?
items.answer: for...of iterates values of iterables (arrays, strings, Map, Set) — maps to C# foreach. for...in iterates enumerable string keys of objects including array indices as strings and inherited keys unless filtered. Never use for...in to walk array elements; use for...of or a classic for loop with an index.
followUps: Does for...of work on plain objects?
items.sixtySeconds: for-of = values (foreach). for-in = keys. Arrays: for-of. Plain objects: Object.entries or for-in with hasOwn.

items.question: How does JavaScript == compare to === and C# ==?
items.answer: === is strict equality without coercion — closest to C# ==. == applies Abstract Equality Comparison with type coercion ("5" == 5 is true). C# == is always strict and typed. TypeScript inherits JS == at run time but lint rules prefer ===.
items.sixtySeconds: Use === in new code. C# == equals JS ===. == coerces — interview trap. null == undefined is true; null === undefined is false.

items.question: What operator precedence traps appear in production?
items.answer: Mixing ?? with || or ?: without parentheses — a ?? b || c parses as (a ?? b) || c. Unary minus vs exponent: -2 ** 2 is -4. + concatenates if either operand is a string. ?? cannot mix with && or || without explicit parentheses in modern syntax rules.
followUps: What does a ?? b ?? c evaluate?
items.sixtySeconds: Parenthesize mixed ?? || ?:. -2**2 = -4. + prefers string concat. ?. stops at null/undefined.

items.question: Why does var in a for loop break async callbacks?
items.answer: var is function-scoped, not block-scoped — one shared binding exists after the loop finishes. Closures capture that final value. let creates a new binding per iteration in for (let i...), so each callback sees the correct index. Same class of bug as classic JavaScript interview questions.
followUps: What is hoisting for var versus let?
items.sixtySeconds: var shares one i after loop. let per iteration fixes closures. var hoists undefined; let TDZ until line.

items.question: What are tagged template literals?
items.answer: A function placed before a template literal receives the static string parts and interpolated values separately: tag`Hello ${name}` calls tag(strings, ...values). Tags power styled-components, GraphQL gql, and sanitizers. String.raw is a built-in tag preserving backslashes.
followUps: How do template literals compare to C# raw strings?
Are template literals safe for HTML?
items.sixtySeconds: Tag gets (strings, ...values). ${} any expression. Not auto-safe for HTML — sanitize or use tags. C# $"{}" ≈ `${}`.
